title: Question 9
stem: Carbon-11 is radioactive and decays by $\beta^{+}$ emission to form boron-11. Carbon-11 has a half-life of 20 minutes. Boron-11 is stable.

parts.label: (a)

markscheme_points.text: time for activity (of sample) to halve

hints: Hint 1: Think about what quantity is halving over time for a radioactive sample - is it mass, count rate, or number of parent nuclei?
parts.proper_answer: The time taken for half of the undecayed nuclei in the sample to decay, or equivalently for the activity of the sample to halve.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What half-life describes**
You are with a sample containing millions of carbon-11 nuclei. You cannot say when any one will decay, but as a whole the activity falls in a predictable way. Half-life is the time scale for that fall.

Step 2: **Precise definition**
So define it as the time taken for the number $N$ of undecayed nuclei to fall to $N/2$, or the time for the activity $A$ to fall to $A/2$. For carbon-11 this is $20\text{ min}$.

hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking about what is present at t = 0 and what happens to the total number of nuclei (carbon + boron) as carbon decays.
Hint 2: Consider how many carbon nuclei remain after one half-life of 20 min, and so how many boron nuclei must have been formed by then.
Hint 3: Think about the shape of the carbon decay curve and what that implies for the rate at which boron is added at early versus late times.
parts.proper_answer: Curve starting at (0,0) rising steeply then flattening towards $N_0$, passing through $(20\text{ min}, 0.5N_0)$, $(40\text{ min}, 0.75N_0)$ and approaching $N_0$ by 80 min.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Start and finish values**
At $t = 0$ there is no boron, so start at $(0,0)$. Boron-11 is stable and every decayed carbon-11 becomes a boron-11, so: $$N_{boron} = N_0 - N_{carbon}$$ As $t$ becomes large, $N_{carbon}$ tends to 0, so $N_{boron}$ tends to $N_0$.

Step 2: **Use half-life points**
After $20\text{ min}$ half the carbon has decayed, so boron is $0.5N_0$. After $40\text{ min}$ only $0.25N_0$ carbon remains, so boron is $0.75N_0$. After $60\text{ min}$ boron is $0.875N_0$. Mark these points.

Step 3: **Shape of the rise**
Join the points with a smooth curve of decreasing gradient that levels off. It is the mirror image of exponential decay - fast rise at first when many carbons are decaying per minute, then almost flat as little carbon is left. Do not draw a straight line.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text: Explain, with reference to the random nature of radioactive decay, why the activity of the carbon-11 sample in **(b)** decreases with time.

markscheme_points.text: every (undecayed) nucleus has the same pr

hints: Hint 1: Recall what random means here - what can you say about the chance of decay in the next minute for any single undecayed carbon nucleus, early or late in the experiment?
Hint 2: Link the total number of decays per second to how many nuclei are still available to decay as time goes on.
parts.proper_answer: Each undecayed nucleus has the same constant probability of decay per unit time. As time passes the number of undecayed nuclei falls, so fewer decays per unit time occur and activity $A = \lambda N$ decreases.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Random but with constant chance**
Random does not mean activity is random. It means each carbon-11 nucleus has the same probability $\lambda$ of decaying in the next second, no matter how long it has already survived.

Step 2: **Fewer nuclei means lower activity**
Activity is the total decay rate: $$A = \lambda N$$ where $N$ is the number of undecayed nuclei present. As decays happen, $N$ gets smaller, so even though $\lambda$ stays constant, the product $\lambda N$ gets smaller. That is why the measured decays per minute fall with time.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: State, with reasons, whether a radiation detector placed near to the sample of carbon-11 indicates a measured count rate from the sample that is less than, the same as or greater than the activity of the sample.

markscheme_points.text: sample emits in all directions but detect
some emissions are absorbed before re
some emissions are scattered within th
some particles may reach detector but
measured count rate is less than the activity

hints: Hint 1: Picture the sample emitting beta-plus particles equally in all directions in space - how much of that sphere does a small detector next to the sample actually cover?
Hint 2: Think about the journey from inside the sample to inside the detector - can every emitted particle survive to be counted?
Hint 3: Consider whether the detector can resolve two particles arriving almost at the same instant as two separate counts.
parts.proper_answer: Measured count rate is less than the activity. Because emission is in all directions so only a fraction reaches the detector, some radiation is absorbed in the sample or air, and the detector has less than 100% efficiency / dead time.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Activity vs count rate**
Activity is the total number of decays per second in the whole sample. Count rate is only the number recorded per second by your detector. The detector cannot catch everything, so count rate < activity.

Step 2: **Geometry misses most particles**
The sample radiates isotropically, in all directions. The detector placed near it subtends only a small solid angle, so most positrons / gamma photons from annihilation miss it completely.

Step 3: **Losses and efficiency**
Even those heading toward the detector may be absorbed or scattered in the sample itself, the container or the air before reaching it. Also the detector does not detect every particle that enters it and cannot resolve particles arriving simultaneously due to dead time, so two decays may give only one count.
